title: Consistency Models
subtitle: Specify which versions a read may return and which histories clients may observe
objectives: Define a consistency model as a contract about what reads may return
Distinguish strong, eventual, and the useful guarantees in between
Recognize which anomaly a user is actually complaining about
Choose the weakest model that keeps your product honest, and know what it costs

exercises.title: A consistency model defines which results concurrent operations may observe
exercises.body: Replicas can hold different versions while updates propagate. A consistency model constrains visible histories: linearizable reads observe the latest completed write in one global order. Eventual consistency guarantees convergence if writes cease and communication continues; replicas may also agree while writes continue.
exercises.note: Tighter constraints require coordination, replica affinity, or version tracking. Those mechanisms add latency, reduce availability during faults, or consume state.

exercises.prompt: Show the minimum components and flows that implement this mechanism: A consistency model defines which results concurrent operations may observe
exercises.why: Replicas can hold different versions while updates propagate. A consistency model constrains visible histories: linearizable reads observe the latest completed write in one global order. Eventual consistency guarantees convergence if writes cease and communication continues; replicas may also agree while writes continue. Tighter constraints require coordination, replica affinity, or version tracking. Those mechanisms add latency, reduce availability during faults, or consume state.

exercises.prompt: A user updates their display name and immediately reads from a lagging replica. Route that user's next read to the leader.
exercises.beforeStatus: USER READ · old display name returned from lagging replica
exercises.afterStatus: USER READ · newly written display name returned from leader
exercises.result: The user's own write became immediately visible
exercises.why: Routing the writer's subsequent read to the write authority provides read-your-writes for that session. Other users can still observe stale replicas, so this narrow session guarantee is not global strong consistency.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: A user updates their display name and immediately reads from a lagging replica. Route that user's next read to the leader. Place Leader, Replica. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: User → Leader; Leader → Replica. That topology is the evidence for the answer: Routing the writer's subsequent read to the write authority provides read-your-writes for that session. Other users can still observe stale replicas, so this narrow session guarantee is not global strong consistency.

exercises.prompt: What is a consistency model, at bottom?
choices: A measure of how reliable a database is
A contract stating which values a read is allowed to return — and therefore which surprises are legal
A setting that makes data more accurate
The number of replicas you keep
exercises.why: A consistency model specifies which values and orderings reads may observe when data has multiple copies. It defines which anomalies the storage system prevents and which application behavior must tolerate.

exercises.prompt: Strong consistency: a write completes, and a read immediately after returns the new value. What does that require?
choices: A read path that can establish current authority or freshness, such as the leader, a valid lease, or a quorum
exercises.why: A linearizable read must not return state older than a completed write. A current leader or valid lease may answer without a new quorum round trip; other protocols use a read quorum or authority check. Quorum writes still coordinate before commitment, and operations block when their required authority is unavailable.

exercises.prompt: Eventual consistency guarantees what, exactly?
choices: If writes stop, all replicas will converge to the same value — with no promise about how long that takes or what you see meanwhile
Reads are correct within one second
exercises.why: Eventual consistency guarantees convergence only if new writes stop and replication can continue. It does not bound replica lag or specify which intermediate value a read returns while updates are propagating.

exercises.prompt: ______ consistency promises replicas converge if writes stop, but says nothing about what you read in the meantime.
exercises.why: Convergence means replicas reach the same value after writes cease and pending updates propagate. The guarantee supplies no time bound, so a long partition can prolong disagreement.

exercises.prompt: Why isn't 'just use strong consistency everywhere' the obvious answer?
choices: It's not supported by most databases
It constrains read and write paths, and operations that cannot establish required authority may wait or fail even when their data could tolerate staleness
exercises.why: A like counter usually tolerates temporary replica differences because no irreversible action depends on an exact current value. Strong consistency would add coordination latency and may reject operations during partitions without materially improving this use case.

exercises.prompt: So what's the design question?
choices: How strong can we afford to be?
What's the weakest model that still keeps the product honest — because the weakest adequate model is the cheapest and most available one
Which model does our database support?
exercises.why: Stronger models forbid more observable reorderings by coordinating more operations, which generally costs latency and partition-time availability. The appropriate model is the weakest one whose permitted anomalies do not violate the product's correctness requirements.

exercises.title: Read-your-writes consistency preserves a client's completed updates
exercises.body: Read-your-writes consistency guarantees that a client session reading an item after its own completed write sees that version or a later one. A service can implement it by routing the session to an up-to-date replica or attaching a version token that reads must satisfy.
exercises.note: This session guarantee does not force other clients to see the update immediately. It prevents one anomaly without paying for a global order on every read.

exercises.prompt: A user posts a comment, then refreshes — and their own comment is gone. Which guarantee were they expecting?
choices: Read-your-writes: you always see your own writes, even if others see them later
exercises.why: Read-your-writes consistency guarantees that a session's later reads include its own successful writes. Routing that user's reads to a replica that has applied the write provides this guarantee while allowing other users to read from lagging replicas.

exercises.prompt: Match each guarantee to the anomaly it forbids.

pairs.right: Your own write vanishing after you make it
Time appearing to run backwards on refresh
Seeing entry 8 of one ordered log without entries 1–7
Seeing a reply before the message it answers

exercises.why: Read-your-writes preserves a session's own completed writes, and monotonic reads prevent that session from moving backward. Consistent-prefix consistency exposes only prefixes of an agreed sequence, such as log entries 1–7 before entry 8. Causal consistency separately preserves happens-before dependencies, such as a question before its reply.

exercises.prompt: Two refreshes: the first shows a new message, the second doesn't. Which guarantee is missing?
choices: Monotonic reads — successive reads should never move backwards in time for one user
exercises.why: The second read reached a replica that had applied fewer updates than the first. Monotonic reads require each session's observed version to stay the same or advance, commonly by pinning the session or tracking a minimum acceptable version.

exercises.prompt: A chat shows a reply before the message it replies to. Which guarantee directly covers that dependency?
choices: Causal consistency — an effect must not appear before the event it depends on
Consistent prefix for an unrelated replicated log
exercises.why: The reply depends on the original post, so causal consistency requires every observer to see the post before the reply. Writes without a dependency may propagate in different orders, avoiding global coordination for unrelated conversations.

exercises.prompt: Why is causal consistency so much cheaper than strong consistency?
choices: It only orders writes that are actually related, leaving unrelated writes to be applied in any order — so most operations need no global agreement
exercises.why: Strong consistency orders operations into one externally coherent history. Causal consistency orders only operations connected by a happens-before dependency, allowing independent writes to replicate concurrently with less coordination.

exercises.prompt: Your product needs users to see their own edits instantly, but is fine if other users see them a second later. What should you buy?
choices: Read-your-writes for the author, eventual for everyone else — that's the actual requirement, precisely stated
exercises.why: The requirement applies to the author's session after a successful post, so read-your-writes is sufficient. Other sessions may read lagging replicas without violating that requirement, avoiding global coordination on every read.

exercises.title: Consistency failures are classified by the operation history a client observed
exercises.body: Diagnose a stale-data report by reconstructing the history: identify the client, its preceding reads and writes, the versions returned, and whether concurrent clients differed. That sequence distinguishes session anomalies from delayed propagation, cache staleness, and application failures.
exercises.note: A replica-affinity fix may restore one client's session ordering while leaving cross-client visibility unchanged. The observed history determines the required guarantee.

exercises.prompt: A user says 'I changed my profile photo and it still shows the old one, but my friend can see the new one.' Diagnosis?
choices: Read-your-writes is missing for this user — their read is hitting a replica that lags behind their own write
exercises.why: The friend's successful read shows that the new photo version exists and has reached at least one serving copy. The author's later session read returned the old photo, violating read-your-writes; routing that session to a sufficiently recent replica or requiring its version token prevents the regression.

exercises.prompt: The source of truth proves a deleted photo reappeared because replica R lagged. Order the observed history.
steps: The source of truth commits deletion as version 12
Replica R remains at version 11, where the photo exists
A later feed read is routed to replica R
Replica R returns version 11 and the old photo reappears
exercises.why: The committed version 12 establishes that deletion persisted, and R's recorded version 11 identifies the lagging copy. Routing the later read to R then explains the reappearance. Without those version and routing facts, the same complaint could also come from a failed delete, restore, retry, stale cache, or asynchronous recreation.

exercises.prompt: A user reports 'the site shows me old data sometimes.' Which could cause it? Select all.
choices: Replication lag on a read replica
A CDN or browser cache serving a stale copy
A search index that hasn't been updated yet
exercises.why: Replicas, caches, and derived indexes can each lag behind the source of truth and return an older value. A slow query is a latency failure because its value remains correct; it does not by itself indicate stale state.

exercises.prompt: Why is 'eventually consistent' a bad answer to give a user or a product manager?
choices: Because it gives no measurable user contract — state a target such as '99.9% visible within one second, with immediate read-your-writes' and define partition behavior
exercises.why: A product requirement must state an observable lag bound and any session guarantees, such as seeing one's own changes immediately. The term eventual consistency alone supplies neither a maximum delay nor defined behavior during propagation.

exercises.prompt: Your team says 'we need strong consistency.' What's the first question to ask?
choices: Which read, by whom, must reflect which write — and what would actually go wrong if it were two seconds late?
How many replicas do we need?
exercises.why: The correct model follows from the exact anomaly and its consequence. A missing own-write may require only read-your-writes, while an anomaly that can create irreversible loss can justify stronger coordination.

exercises.prompt: Classify each concrete complaint before choosing a repair.

pairs.left: The like count moved backward on refresh
I see a reply before its source message
The page took 8 seconds to load
pairs.right: Latency problem, not a consistency anomaly

exercises.why: Consistency diagnosis depends on the observed operation history: losing one's own write, moving to an older observed version, or revealing an effect before its cause violate different contracts. An eight-second response concerns timing; it can still return a value allowed by the consistency model.

exercises.title: Overlapping read and write quorums expose at least one acknowledged copy
exercises.body: For a fixed set of `N` replicas, acknowledge a write after `W` replicas store it and query `R` replicas per read. When `W + R > N`, every completed write quorum intersects every read quorum, so the read contacts at least one replica that accepted the write.
exercises.note: Intersection alone does not identify the newest version or order concurrent writes. The system still needs version comparison, conflict handling, or consensus.

exercises.prompt: For one fixed set of N=3 replicas, build read and write paths whose quorums must overlap.
exercises.why: The write completes after two of three replicas store it, and each read queries two of the same three replicas. Because `W + R = 4 > 3`, those sets share at least one copy of the completed write. If both paths used one replica, they could be disjoint and the read could return stale data; overlap still needs version comparison and write ordering to provide linearizability.

exercises.prompt: Build the end-to-end path required by this scenario: For one fixed set of N=3 replicas, build read and write paths whose quorums must overlap.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Client Write → Store on W = 2; Store on W = 2 → Replica Set; Client Read → Query R = 2; Query R = 2 → Replica Set. That topology is the evidence for the answer: The write completes after two of three replicas store it, and each read queries two of the same three replicas. Because `W + R = 4 > 3`, those sets share at least one copy of the completed write. If both paths used one replica, they could be disjoint and the read could return stale data; overlap still needs version comparison and write ordering to provide linearizability.

exercises.prompt: Same 3 replicas, but W=1 and R=1. What did you buy and lose?
choices: Fast writes and fast reads that stay available if replicas are down — and no overlap guarantee, so a read can easily miss the newest write
exercises.why: With `W=1`, `R=1`, and `N=3`, the read and write sets can be disjoint, so a read may return an older value. One reachable replica can still serve each operation, providing low latency and higher availability at the cost of freshness.

exercises.prompt: You're atomically reserving the last item during checkout for a limited product drop. Slide toward your model.
exercises.why: An inventory reservation authorizes a sale, so concurrent attempts for the last item must be ordered against the same current stock state. Coordination adds latency and may refuse requests during faults, but it prevents two successful reservations from consuming one unit. A display-only count could instead tolerate bounded staleness.

exercises.prompt: Someone proposes 'use timestamps — the newest write wins.' What's the flaw?
choices: Different machines' clocks disagree, so 'newest' depends on whose clock you believe — and a skewed clock can silently discard a genuinely later write
exercises.why: Physical clocks on different nodes drift and can be corrected, so timestamps may not reflect causal or real-time write order. A fast clock can make one value win later conflicts; logical clocks or version vectors track event order without assuming synchronized wall clocks.

exercises.prompt: Can one product use several consistency models at once?
choices: Yes, and it should: payments strong, profile edits read-your-writes, feeds eventual — each dataset gets the weakest model that keeps it honest
exercises.why: Consistency requirements apply to particular operations and data. A system can coordinate balances strongly while replicating feeds eventually, matching each model's latency and availability cost to the consequence of an anomaly.

exercises.prompt: What's the honest summary of consistency models?
choices: Stronger is better; use the strongest you can afford
They're contracts about what a read may return: stronger forbids more surprises and costs coordination, so pick the weakest model that keeps the product honest — per dataset, not per company
exercises.why: A consistency model defines which disagreement among copies may reach a read. Stronger guarantees exclude more anomalies through coordination, while weaker guarantees can reduce latency and remain available through more failures; requirements should select the minimum sufficient guarantee.

exercises.prompt: A user edits a document title, then immediately reloads and sees the old title from another replica. Which session guarantee is missing?
choices: Global total order for every user
exercises.why: The user's own later read failed to include their completed write. Read-your-writes can be provided through sticky routing, version tokens, or waiting for a sufficiently advanced replica.
